Walk the truck before it rolls: A / D or the arrow keys (or the ◀ ▶ buttons) take you round it, C climbs into the cab.
Click a marked item to get a proper look at it. Decide: pass it (P), or flag the defect (F).

Some checks need a test first (T): switch the lights and hazards on in the cab (L) before judging any lamp, press the horn, hold the brake, pull on the latches, and gauge the tires. Tread minimum: 4/32" on a steer (front) tire, 2/32" on the others.
Flagging good parts costs you too. Look properly, then decide.
Front tire, driver side
Tread deep and even across the width, no cuts or bulges.
Tread worn down to the wear bars — well under the legal minimum.
A bald steer tire hydroplanes in the first rain and can blow out under load. That is an out-of-service defect.
A steer (front) tire needs at least 4/32" of tread; the others at least 2/32". Gauge it, don't guess.
Rear tire, driver side
Good depth, even wear, valve cap in place.
A gouge in the sidewall, down into the cords.
A sidewall cut can let go without warning at highway speed.
Sidewall damage is a defect even when the tread looks fine.
Under the truck
Dry ground under the engine and driveline.
Fresh oil dripping from the engine with a puddle forming.
An engine that loses its oil seizes, usually in traffic, usually expensively.
Look at the ground under the truck before you move it. A wet patch is the cheapest warning you will ever get.
Driver mirror
Clean, tight, and showing the side of the truck and the lane behind.
Knocked out of position — it shows sky and your own door.
A mirror pointing at nothing is a blind spot you cannot check while changing lanes.
Set your mirrors before you move, and reset them if the truck was parked by someone else.
Fuel cap
Cap fitted and sealed.
Cap missing, with fuel residue down the side of the tank.
Fuel splashes out on corners: a fire risk, a spill, and a fuel bill.
Check the cap is on and sealed after every fill.
Front tire, curb side
Good depth and even wear.
Badly worn on one edge — the alignment is out.
Uneven wear ruins tires fast and reduces grip on the worn edge.
Gauge a tire in more than one place: one edge can be bald while the other looks fine.
Entry steps
Clean, dry, grip surface intact.
Greasy film across the bottom step.
That is the step you use two hundred times a day. It is the single most common way couriers fall.
Keep the steps clean and dry, and use three points of contact every time.
Curb-side door latch
Latches and holds firmly.
The latch does not seat — the door can swing open.
A door that opens on a turn can strike a cyclist or dump freight into the street.
Test every latch by pulling on it, not by looking at it.
Headlight, driver side
Bright and clear, lens intact.
Dead — cracked lens with moisture inside.
One headlight at dusk means you are half as visible and it is a citation.
Switch the lights and hazards on in the cab, then walk around and check every lamp yourself.
Turn signal, curb side
Amber, bright, flashing evenly.
Dead lamp.
A dead signal means the cars around you do not know where you are going.
Signals are the only thing telling traffic your intentions. Check them both.
Windshield
Clean, no cracks in the swept area.
A star crack spreading in the driver's line of sight.
Cracks spread with heat and vibration, and one in your sight line is an out-of-service defect.
Damage in the swept area of the windshield is a defect, however small it starts.
Wiper blades
Rubber intact, sitting flat on the glass.
Rubber perished and lifting away from the blade.
Discover this in the first downpour and you are driving blind.
Check wipers on a dry day. Nobody wants to find out in the rain.
Tail light, driver side
Bright red, lens intact.
Dead lamp with a cracked lens.
Being rear-ended at a stop is exactly what tail lights prevent.
Walk to the back with the lights on. You cannot check a tail light from the cab.
Cargo door
Runs freely, latches and locks.
The latch does not seat properly.
A cargo door that opens on the road scatters freight across a lane.
Open and close the cargo door as part of the walkaround, every day.
Rear reflector
Clean and intact.
Cracked and filthy — no reflection left.
At night, reflectors are what stop a driver from hitting a parked truck.
Reflectors and reflective tape are required equipment, not decoration.
Horn
Loud and immediate.
Nothing — the horn is dead.
The horn is how you warn a pedestrian stepping out behind you while backing.
Test the horn. It only matters on the day you need it.
Seat belt
Webbing sound, latches firmly, retracts.
Webbing frayed most of the way through.
A frayed belt tears in the crash it was supposed to save you from.
Pull the belt all the way out and look along the webbing for fraying and cuts.
Service brake
Firm pedal that holds.
The pedal sinks slowly under steady pressure.
A sinking pedal means the brakes will not be there when you need them hardest.
Hold steady pressure on the pedal. It should stay put, not creep toward the floor.
Oil pressure gauge
Reading in the normal band, warning lamp out.
Reading low at idle, with the oil warning lamp lit.
Low oil pressure can wreck the engine or stall it in traffic.
Let the gauges come up to normal before you move, and never drive with a warning lamp lit.
Fire extinguisher
Charged, tagged, and secured in its bracket.
Needle in the red and the inspection tag is missing.
A discharged extinguisher is the same as no extinguisher.
Check the gauge and the inspection tag, not just that it is there.
Warning triangles
Full set of three, stowed and intact.
Only one triangle in the kit.
Broken down on a shoulder with no warning devices is how a stopped truck gets hit.
Carry the full set of emergency warning devices, and know where they are.
Anything you miss on the walkaround rolls out of the yard with you.
Flagging good parts takes a truck out of service for nothing. Look properly before you flag.
Every defect caught and nothing good condemned — that is exactly what the walkaround is for.

Commitments come first. Sequence the timed stops, then fill the gaps with the flexible ones — never the other way round.
Arriving before a pickup is ready is a wasted trip. Build the window into the order instead of sitting at the dock doing nothing.
A pickup you reach after the dock closes is a missed pickup — the customer ships with someone else tomorrow.
Plan loops, not zig-zags. Group stops by block and leave the far corner for the way back.
Check closures before you sequence. A shut block can turn two "next door" stops into a six-block detour.
The school zone is slow while it is active. Early in the day, work around it and come back later.
Clean plan: every commitment met on the shortest sensible loop. That is what dispatch is looking for.
You drive a loaded van: W accelerate, S brake, A/D turn the wheel (hold it with W to turn). It is heavy: brake early, and pull forward before a right turn so the back wheels clear the curb.

Mirrors, signal, then move: M checks the mirrors, Q and E are the indicators (left, right), for every turn and every pull-out. In D the van creeps: hold SPACE to wait. R changes gear at a standstill. B belt · L lights · G look before backing.
P parks: inside the marked bay, close to the curb, straight, facing the way the traffic goes.
Six checkpoints across town. Between them, things happen: a ball, a door, a bus, standing water. Everything is judged on what you actually do, and the weather turns halfway.
Your handheld buzzes
The handheld buzzes in its cradle — a customer message.
You left it alone. Nothing on that screen is worth the road.
You worked the handheld while rolling.
Handle messages parked, not at the wheel and not at red lights — traffic and people move while you read.
Ball in the street
A ball bounces out into the road ahead.
You were down to walking pace before the child came out. That is the whole lesson.
You were still carrying speed when a child came out after that ball.
You hit a child chasing a ball.
Near homes, schools and parks, cover the brake. A ball in the street means a child is about to follow it.
Car door
Someone is sitting in that parked car.
You gave that door room. Good lane position.
You went past that opening door far too close and too fast.
You took a parked car's door off.
Give parked cars about three feet and watch for heads, brake lights and doors — assume every one of them is about to open.
Standing water
Standing water across the road ahead.
Off the gas, wheel straight, no panic braking. The tires found the road again.
You braked or steered hard with no grip under you — that is how a van ends up sideways.
If you hydroplane: ease off the accelerator, hold the wheel straight and do not brake hard until the tires bite again.
Distracted pedestrian
Someone on their phone is drifting toward the crossing.
You slowed and let them go. They never looked up once.
You kept your speed at a crossing with someone stepping into it.
You hit a pedestrian in a crosswalk.
Never assume a pedestrian has seen you. Slow down, cover the brake and be ready to give up the right of way.
School bus
School bus ahead, red lights flashing and the stop arm coming out.
Stopped and stayed stopped until the arm folded in. Exactly right.
You passed a stopped school bus with its red lights flashing.
Stop for a school bus with flashing red lights. On an undivided road that includes oncoming traffic — kids cross from either side.
Last stop
Last leg. If you ever have to back up, stop and get out and look first (G).
Avoid backing when you can. When you cannot: G.O.A.L. — get out and look — then back slowly on your mirrors.
Calm, defensive and decisive the whole way. That is what a good route looks like.
Scan far enough ahead that you are slowing early instead of braking late.
Five short clips. The van drives itself: your job is to watch the road like a courier.
Press SPACE (or click) the moment you see a hazard STARTING to develop, not when it is already in front of you.
The earlier you spot it, the more points: up to 5 a clip. Pressing over and over scores nothing.
Parked cars, a quiet street
A ball rolling out from between parked cars: a child is very likely to follow it. Cover the brake the moment you see the ball.
Driveways on the right
Reverse lights on a car in a driveway: it is about to back out, and the driver may not see a van. Ease off and be ready to stop.
A pedestrian heading for the crossing with their eyes on their phone may step out without looking. Slow down before the crossing.
A line of parked cars
Someone sitting in a parked car with the brake lights on may open the door into the road. Give parked cars a door's width.
A junction ahead
A car coming up to the side street's stop sign too fast to stop: be ready for it to roll out in front of you.
Eyes up and early every time: the earlier you see a hazard developing, the more time you have to deal with it.
Watch for the clue before the hazard: a ball before a child, reverse lights before a reversing car, a phone before a step into the road.
Click a package (or press SPACE for the one at the front) to scan it. The scan tells you the bin.
Then drag it into that bin, or press the bin's number: the keys send the package you scanned (the glowing one). A bin keeps its number all shift.
Sorting a piece you never scanned is a guess, and guesses cost you.

Wave 1 · Scan, then sort
Scan a package to read its label, then match the route code (R1, R2, R3) to its bin.
PRI
New Rule · Priority
An orange PRIORITY band goes to the Priority bin — no matter what route it says.
EXC
New Rule · Exceptions
Crushed or leaking? Pull it to Exceptions — even if it is priority. Damaged freight never goes down the line.
New Rule · Dangerous goods
A hazard diamond means the DG cage, segregated from everything else. A damaged DG piece is worse, not better: that one goes to Exceptions and gets reported.
HVY
New Rule · Heavy pieces
50 lb and over goes down the heavy chute for a team lift. Swinging one into a route bin on your own is how backs get hurt.
Scan before you sort. The label is the only thing that knows where a piece is going — your memory of the last one does not.
Damaged or leaking packages go to Exceptions — never down the line, even when they are marked priority.
Dangerous goods ride in the DG cage, segregated. A damaged DG piece is an exception and a report, not a repack.
Anything 50 lb or over goes down the heavy chute for a team lift. No single-person hero lifts on a belt.
Priority overrides the route code. Check for priority markings before you read the route.
Read the label before you let go — one mis-sort puts a package on the wrong truck and makes it late.
Keep a steady rhythm. A package that rides off the end becomes a late delivery.
Clear a jam the moment it happens. Everything behind it backs up while you stand there.
Clean sort. Scan, read, send — that is how the pros keep a belt moving.
Five loads, one back. First size up each load and choose how to move it.
Then do the lift yourself. Keys: A / D to step, S to bend your knees, W to straighten up, SPACE to grip and to let go. Mouse: hold the arrow pad under the gauge, and click GRIP.
Your back hinges over whatever your knees and your distance leave it — watch the SPINE LOAD gauge and keep it under the line.
Time spent over that line drains your Back Health. Protect it — it has to last a whole career.
Small parts box
A 12 lb box on the floor needs to go on the pallet behind you.
Lift it myself — with good form
Light, compact load: a solo lift with good form is the right call.
Radio a coworker to help
Safe, but overkill for 12 lb. Save team lifts for heavy or awkward loads.
Case of copy paper
A 40 lb case of paper. Compact, with good hand-holds.
A compact 40 lb case is manageable solo for most people — form is everything.
Grab a hand truck
Never wrong to use equipment! Slightly slower for one compact box, but zero strain.
Just bend over and yank it up fast
Bending at the waist and jerking a load is a classic back injury. Plan the lift and use your legs.
Long flat-pack box
A 6-foot flat-pack box. Not very heavy, but long and hard to balance.
Team lift — get a coworker on the other end
Awkward loads are as risky as heavy ones. A second person keeps it balanced and close.
Grab it in the middle and wing it
Long loads swing and twist your spine. Get help for awkward loads — then lift together.
Machine part crate
A 95 lb crate marked HEAVY. It needs to go across the floor to the pallet.
Use a hand truck
Exactly. Let equipment carry heavy loads — your back isn't a forklift.
Team lift with a coworker
Better than solo, but a hand truck is safer for both of you when one is available.
Lift it solo — I've got this
Heavy loads beyond what you can safely handle alone call for equipment or help. No heroics.
Box on the top shelf
A 25 lb box sits on a shelf above your head.
Use a step stool so the box is at chest height
Bringing yourself up to the load avoids lifting overhead, where you have the least control.
Reach up and pull it down over my head
Lifting overhead strains shoulders and back — and boxes fall on faces. Use a stool or platform.
Climb the shelving
Shelving isn't a ladder. Falls are one of the most common workplace injuries. Use a proper step stool.
Get close to the load before lifting — reaching out multiplies the strain on your back.
Bend at the knees, not the waist. Keep your back straight as you go down.
Get a firm grip and tighten your core before the load leaves the ground.
Lift smoothly with your legs. Jerky, fast lifts are how backs get hurt.
Step your feet round to face where the load is going — reaching and twisting under a load is how discs go.
Lower the load the same way you lifted it: bend your knees and set it down under control.
Plan every lift. Even a "quick" lift done bent over can injure your back.
Awkward or long loads need a team lift, even if they aren't very heavy.
Use a hand truck or get help for heavy loads — no heroics.
Avoid lifting above shoulder height. Use a step stool or platform.
Never climb shelving — use a proper step stool or ladder.
Textbook lifting! Close, knees bent, back straight, smooth, pivot — every single time.
Turn every package before you move it: A / D turn it round, W shows the top, S shows the base — or click the six face dots.
Marks hide on the sides, the top and underneath. Deciding before you have seen all six sides is a blind call, and it is scored as one.
Drag the package onto the right handling station (or press its number, 1-6). If more than one mark applies, the most restrictive one wins.

Fragile
Breakable contents. Handle gently, never stack heavy freight on top.
This Way Up
Orientation arrows, usually on two opposite sides. Keep them pointing up.
Keep Dry
Protect from rain and wet surfaces — including the wet floor of a van.
Class 3 · Flammable Liquid
Dangerous goods. Cage it, segregate it, and check the paperwork.
Class 8 · Corrosive
Damages skin and metal. Dangerous goods handling.
Class 5.1 · Oxidizer
Intensifies fire. Never beside flammables. Dangerous goods handling.
Class 2 · Gas
Compressed gas (green = non-flammable). Dangerous goods handling.
Class 9 · Misc. DG
Dry ice, magnetised material, batteries. Looks harmless, still DG.
Lithium Battery Mark
Cells inside. A damaged one can overheat — handle per battery rules.
Class 9 · Lithium Batteries
Nothing but a shipping label on any of the six sides — standard handling. You still checked, which is the point.
Broken-glass symbol on the front: fragile shelf, and nothing goes on top of it.
Two arrows over a bar = orientation marks. It rides upright on the cart, never on its side.

Explain that the delay wasn't your fault
Acknowledge it, then say what you can do
Give them the depot number and move on
Promise them it will arrive later today
A calm voice and acknowledging the problem de-escalate. Then offer what you actually can do. Don't promise what you can't.
At a business, a receptionist signs for a package addressed to a colleague. Whose name do you record?
The addressee's, since it is their package
The receptionist's, as they printed it
The company's name from the label
Nobody's: the scan alone is enough
Record the printed name of whoever actually signed, even when it isn't the addressee.
A signature-required package, and nobody answers the door. You…
Leave it somewhere hidden and take a photo
Record an exception and leave a door tag
Sign for it yourself so the customer gets it
Leave it with the neighbor next door
A signature-required package is never left unattended. Record the exception, leave a door tag and keep the package.
A customer wants to chat and you are behind schedule. You should…
Cut them off and walk back to the van
Stay friendly, then close it politely
Explain how many stops you still have left
Keep working and ignore them until they stop
Stay friendly and warm but brief. Different customers need different styles; all of them deserve courtesy.
A customer is aggressive and you feel unsafe. What do you do?
Stand your ground and argue your side firmly
Get to safety, don't engage, and report it
Finish the delivery quickly, whatever happens
Calm them down by giving them the package
Your safety comes first. Leave, don't escalate, and report it to your manager.
The label says Maple Court, but you are on Maple Avenue, where the number doesn't exist. You…
Deliver to the closest number on the avenue
Check the address, then ask dispatch instead of guessing
Leave it at the corner shop for them to collect
Mark it delivered and sort it out tomorrow
"Close enough" is not an address. Verify it, and ask dispatch rather than guess.
A package arrives crushed with the contents showing. What do you do?
Tape it back up neatly and deliver it
Photograph it and follow the damage procedure
Remove the broken part and deliver the rest
Deliver it as it is and say nothing about it
Document it and follow the damage procedure, so the customer and the claim are handled properly.
A severe storm warning comes in mid-route. The right call is…
Speed up to finish the route before it hits
Follow dispatch and shelter if told to
Keep driving, since the van will protect you
Switch your phone off so you can concentrate
No package is worth your life. Follow instructions, shelter when told, and resume only when it is safe.
The customer's note asks you to leave the package somewhere unsafe (in the road view, in the rain). You…
Follow the note exactly: it is their choice
Pick a safe spot close to it and record where
Take it back to the depot for a redelivery
Leave it at the curb where they can see it
Follow delivery instructions when it is safe to. If not, choose a safe, sensible spot and record it.
You find a package for the wrong stop on your shelves. When is the best time to catch this?
At the door, when you read the label
Before it leaves the van, when you scan
At the end of the day, when you check in
When the customer calls to say it is missing
Scan every package before it leaves the truck. The scan catches wrong-stop packages.
What should a proof-of-delivery photo show?
The package and the house number beside it
The package and the spot where it was left
The customer holding the package at the door
Only the package and its label, close up
The package and where it was left. Never a house number, and never people or any part of one, yours included.
An adult-signature (21+) delivery: the person at the door has an expired ID. You…
Accept it, as long as the photo matches them
Keep it and record the ID exception
Ask an adult neighbor to sign for them
Leave it at the door with a photo
Adult signature needs a valid, unexpired government photo ID and 21 or older. No exceptions.
Nobody is home for a package that needs a signature. Which is right?
A photo delivery at the front door
An exception, a door tag, back on the truck
Sign for them, since you know it's the right house
Leave it with the building's cleaner or super
Nobody home + signature required = exception, door tag, and the package stays on the truck.
Why knock or ring before leaving a package?
You don't need to for a photo delivery
Many customers would rather have it handed over
Only for heavy packages they can't lift
Only when the delivery note asks you to
Always attempt contact first. Many customers would rather receive the package in person.
The business is closed at your delivery time. You…
Leave it at the door in the doorway
Record "business closed" and bring it back
Slide it through the mail slot if it fits
Ask the shop next door to hold it for them
A closed business is an exception: record it and bring the package back.
How should the day's packages be loaded on the shelves?
Biggest first, so the small ones fit around them
In stop order, with the next stop nearest to hand
Alphabetically by street, so they're easy to find
In any order: the scanner will find them
Load in stop order. Searching the shelves at every stop costs minutes each time.
Where do the heaviest packages go?
On the top shelf, so they don't crush others
Low down, on the bottom shelves or the floor
By the door, so they are easy to unload
Anywhere there is room left for them
Heavy goes low: it is safer to lift and keeps the van stable.
Why secure the load before driving?
A tidy van is quicker to inspect at the depot
Loose packages shift, break and fall on you
It is only needed on long highway routes
So the scanner can read every label
A secured load doesn't shift under braking or cornering, and nothing falls on you when you open the door.
At a stop, you can't find the package quickly. What is the lesson?
Search harder and faster at every stop
Load each stop together, labels out
Skip the stop and come back to it later
Deliver a different package there instead
A good load is found fast: sequence, group by stop, and keep labels facing out.
A fragile package should be…
Under the heavy boxes, where it can't slide
On top or in its own spot, never under weight
On the floor by the door, ready to go
Carried in your hands all day long
Never put weight on fragile packages. Protect them on top or in their own spot.
At a business pickup, a package is badly taped and half open. You…
Take it and fix the packing at the depot
Refuse it until it is properly packed
Take it, but leave it out of your scans
Tape it up yourself and accept it
What you accept, you own. Refuse packages that aren't properly packed.
An international shipment's commercial invoice is missing the contents' value. What happens?
It ships anyway: customs works it out
Customs can hold it: complete it first
You write in your best guess of the value
Nothing: customs only checks the weight
Customs needs a full description, value and currency. Incomplete paperwork means delays or returns.
The shipper says a box "just has some batteries and a bit of paint" but it isn't declared. You…
Accept it: a small amount doesn't count
Refuse it unless it is properly declared
Accept it, and keep it away from other boxes
Take the batteries out, then accept the rest
Dangerous goods (some batteries, flammable paint) must be declared and packed to the rules. Undeclared: refuse.
Before leaving a pickup, you should…
Count the pieces and scan every one
Trust the shipper's count on the paperwork
Scan one piece from each stack to save time
Load them now and scan them at the depot
Count and scan every piece at pickup, so the count matches the paperwork before you drive away.
A package has a hazard diamond label you don't recognize. What do you do?
Treat it as ordinary freight until told otherwise
Check the handling rules, or ask before moving it
Peel the label off so it doesn't confuse anyone
Put it with the fragile packages, to be safe
Hazard diamonds carry handling rules. If in doubt, check or ask before you move it.
Icy porch steps and a package in your arms. How do you climb them?
Quickly, so you spend less time on the ice
Slowly, in short steps, watching your feet
Toss the package onto the porch, then climb
Two at a time, holding the package tight
Slow down on ice and wet steps: short, careful steps, a hand free if you can. Most falls happen while carrying something.
A dog is barking and growling at the gate. You should…
Go in quickly and calmly so it settles
Stay outside the gate and wait for the owner
Hold out a hand so it can smell you
Run back to the van before it gets out
Never enter a yard with an aggressive dog. Keep something between you and the dog, make noise, wait or reattempt, and don't run.
On a hot day, when should you drink water?
Whenever you start to feel thirsty
Regularly, before you feel thirsty
At lunch, so you don't lose time
As soon as you start to feel dizzy
Hydrate before you are thirsty and take shade breaks. Dizziness and confusion mean heat illness: stop and get help.
After a minor collision, what should you NOT do?
Check whether anyone has been hurt
Admit fault to the other driver
Take photographs of both vehicles
Call it in to your manager straight away
Never admit fault at the scene. Check on people, photograph everything, exchange details and call it in.
A garden hose lies across the path to the door. What is best?
Step over it carefully with the package
Set the package down and move it aside
Walk around it across the lawn instead
Kick it out of the way as you walk
Clear trip hazards off the walkway, even with a package in hand: set it down, move them, pick it up.
